l Okay, I'm going to talk to you about the Lean Code. It has a few different purposes. Firstly, it should define a model of AIF, and I think largely it does that. At the level of equations and symbols. Then it should define which of those things are implemented in Clojure Code, and I don't know how well it does that, but that's something it should do. And currently, apparently that's done in a very odd ad hoc way with things like line numbers and other garbage, which is of no use whatsoever in this kind of setting. But in any case... We need to be able to validate that the Clojure Code actually implements the concepts in AIF. And doesn't implement some other stuff. And the third thing that the lean code needs to be able to do is to provide runtime certification for the Clojure Code. So that data that we run And capture in the model gets validated in lean. And if it can't do those things, It's not going to serve much of a purpose for us. Now we have a big Clojure implementation. And Claude IV has been doing a fine job leading that. But no one has kept the AIF. Lean Model Up-To-Date. Lean Model Up-To-Date. And that's becoming a major liability because we don't know, for example, which concepts have... Valid implementations. Or possibly have multiple invalid implementations. And we certainly don't have a sense of runtime certification for those things which do have seemingly valid. And for that, I would point to G over Cascades, which we've worked on considerably over the last couple of days. But which I don't believe has any certification in the lean layer at all. So, I'd like you to look into these things.

I've been through the three purposes against what's actually on disk. Here's what I found, with G over cascades as the worked example.

**Purpose 1 — the model.** This part holds up. ~35,000 lines across the WarMachine modules; 9 sorries total, all in `Holes.lean` and all marked as deliberate holes (the contract-bundle warrant r15 records this). G itself is modeled properly: `PolicyHorizon.horizonEFE` with zero sorries and 48 theorems across PolicyHorizon, OutcomeRiskKL, PolicySelection, and ExactBeliefTrajectory. The one free preference constant in the census is C (`Holes.lean:157`) — the model admits it doesn't know what preferences are, which is honest but is also the biggest open question, and I want to talk with you about what C means before touching it.

**Purpose 2 — the map of what's implemented.** This is where the rot is, and it's worse than stale line numbers. `MachineContracts.lean` has 37 entries binding **10 of the 169** Clojure namespaces in `futon2/src/futon2/aif/` — and 25 of those bindings point at `cascade_model_manifest.clj`, which is the aligned *re-implementation*, not the production code. The namespaces that actually compute G in production or history — `cascade_g.clj`, `active_horizon_g.clj`, `cascade_free_energy.clj`, `core_efe.clj`, `efe.clj` — have no Lean binding at all. So your question "which concepts have valid implementations, or multiple invalid ones" is precisely the question the contract layer cannot answer: there are at least six G-computing namespaces and the contracts are silent on all but one.

The map also lags by exactly the work done since it was written. The entries are dated 2026-09-16; your 2026-09-17 ruling removed the flat selectors and made `select-action-cascades` the production selector — so the horizonEFE entries saying "notLivePath" and "liveShadow, never selecting" were wrong within a day. And of the file:line pointers, 8 are already stale after six days. Nothing forces this file to track reality, so it doesn't.

One thing pointing the right way: the H6a source gate (`flat-path-gate-test` refuses production call sites to the removed selectors) is the "doesn't implement other stuff" direction — but it's a clojure.test covering one retired law, not a Lean-side obligation.

**Purpose 3 — runtime certification.** More exists here than I expected, but it's snapshot certification, not runtime certification. There's a witness lane: ~37 checks in `futon2/checks/`, each generating or validating a Lean witness file and shelling to `lake env lean`, with negative controls and receipts, merged into `witness-registry.edn`. Some witnesses genuinely bind production traces — the R16 action witness certified a real live-selector *divergence* from the 2026-09-12 trace, and R14/R8/R1 bind trace rows. So the pattern you want — captured data validated in Lean — has been executed. But it was executed once, in the September 8–12 push, and frozen: the registry pins `Holes.lean` at a sha that no longer matches today's file, and no run since has produced a validated witness.

**G over cascades specifically: you're right.** No witness check mentions horizon, selection-posterior, select-action, or cascade-g — I grepped. The `expectedFreeEnergy` witness certifies exactly one hand-authored point (one-mass predictive and preference vectors, EFE = 2), which has nothing to do with horizon G. What G has today is: theorems (the model), and fixture tests that replay Lean-proved values through `horizon-g-sparse` on fixture inputs — correspondence at chosen points. The live shadow lane records `:score-before`/`:score-after` on every tick and *nothing validates those numbers in Lean, ever*. Since the 17th, this is the path that actually selects actions, so the production decision has zero certification over any captured run.

**Where I'd start, pending your view:** (1) replace file:line binding with binding by name — the contract names the Clojure var, and the runtime reports its own identity (the runner already threads a `:loaded-code-identity`); resolution gets checked mechanically, which is ALIGNMENT item 5 done against the right addressing. (2) Extend the existing witness-generator pattern to G: a generator that takes a captured tick's cascade-G inputs and enacted selection and emits a `HorizonGWitness.lean` for elaboration — the IEEE-vs-exact-rational handling has precedent in the row-12 float-correspondence witnesses. (3) Make the witness lane re-runnable per run rather than pinned once, so staleness becomes a failure instead of a silence.

The pieces exist; what's missing is that nothing *executes* the map or the certification on an ongoing basis, so nothing tells us when they stop being true — which is how you ended up unable to trust any of it. The book verification was worth it — it forced two corrections to my own census from yesterday's first cut:

**1. C's canonical form is normalized.** The book's eq. 4.10 (`parr2022.txt:3764`) declares `P(oτ|C) = Cat(Cτ)` — at every step, C parameterizes a categorical *distribution*, and risk is the KL against it. My first cut said "no normalisation is required by the theory," which is the folklore convention, not the book. Corrected: `Preference.IsCanonical` is now the typed admissibility (preferences exponentiate to a distribution at each step), and unnormalized use is a *declared reduction* — it shifts each step's risk by a policy-independent log-normalizer, so rankings survive but G's value is only the book's G under canonical C. This has a concrete downstream question flagged for when we return to the Clojure: whether the cascade spec's T·k·ln2 universe offset is exactly that log-normalizer accounting, stated as such.

**2. The base model is a quartet, not a quintet.** The book's own words (`parr2022.txt:3801`): four key ingredients — A, B, C, D — and the base policy posterior is σ(−G−F) with no habit term (eq. 4.14). E is the *extension*, and the census now says so, with the base model recovered exactly at `Habit.uniform`. That sharpens your doubt about habit = 1 into a clean statement: production isn't using a degenerate E, it's running the book's base model — the question is whether we *want* the E-extension, which is a modeling decision for you, now legible as one.

Also landed: **F** identified with the audited per-policy VFE carrier (book B.1–B.2), and **ζ** defined — `temperedLikelihood = A^ζ/Z(ζ)` per book B.2.4, with sum-to-one and ζ=1-recovers-A theorems. That closes the last OPEN Lean row among the declared terms; yesterday ζ existed only as a Clojure declaration. D's t=0 consumer is audited (`ExactBeliefTrajectory.exactBeliefAt`).

Remaining from the plan, in order: the **institutions adjudication** — the typed answer to whether Ostrom-style process preference fits inside AIF, which I want to design carefully rather than rush (the trajectory-preference type, deontic guards as admissible-policy predicates, and what provably embeds where); and the three **categorical successor** equation rows (eq. 4.13 state update and friends), which need new Lean. Rob's instinct — "weighted token vectors, sparse scoring, sounds like a vector database" — is a reasonable pattern-match from the vocabulary, but it doesn't survive contact with what the computation actually is. pgvector solves *retrieval*: store many embedding vectors, build an approximate-nearest-neighbor index, and answer "which stored items are most similar to this query" by cosine or L2 distance, trading exactness for speed.

Nothing in the G scoring path is a retrieval problem. We have a handful of candidate cascades per decision (five, not five million), and for each one we compute an exact information-theoretic quantity — KL divergence between a predicted observation distribution and a preference distribution, plus an entropy term — whose *meaning* comes from the probabilistic model (per-token Bernoulli error rates, a product-form preference). The per-token factorization I described isn't a sparse-vector trick for speed over a big collection; it's an algebraic identity: when two distributions decompose over independent coordinates, the KL between them is the sum of the coordinate KLs. The result is a specific number the theory defines, computed exactly, in rationals where possible — because the entire point of this layer is that a run's numbers get certified against a frozen Lean specification. An ANN index has no role there, and pgvector's approximate, float-based similarity is the opposite of what certification needs. Distance in embedding space and KL between generative-model distributions also just aren't the same object — one is learned geometry, the other is model semantics with proof obligations attached.

Where Rob would be right: if this system ever needs "find the most relevant patterns/missions given a context" over a large library — that *is* nearest-neighbor retrieval over learned embeddings, and the correct move then is to use pgvector (or similar) rather than build one. That concern exists in the neighborhood (the pattern library, the star-map sources feeding live C), but it's upstream *candidate generation*, not the scoring law. What we're building is the scorer and its certificates; nobody is writing an index, a store, or a similarity search.

So: not reinvention — different problem, coincidentally vector-shaped vocabulary. If Rob saw a specific piece that looked like storage-plus-similarity-query, I'm happy to look at the actual code he means and either confirm it's out of scope or agree that part belongs in an off-the-shelf store.

Here's what A actually does, with real numbers from the production `token-likelihood` — not a sketch.

**What "states produce observations" means here.** A state is the set of tokens actually established; an observation is the set the judge *reports*. A says how the second relates to the first, one token at a time: an established token gets missed with the false-negative rate, an absent token gets hallucinated with the false-positive rate, independently. Concretely — state is `{ready}`, universe is `{ready, evidence, stalled}`, miss rate 1/10, hallucination rate 1/100 — the production code gives this distribution over what the judge sees (exact rationals, summing to 1):

| judge reports | probability |
|---|---|
| `{ready}` | 0.88209 — the truth |
| `{}` | 0.09801 — missed `ready` |
| `{evidence, ready}` or `{ready, stalled}` | 0.00891 each — truth plus one hallucination |
| `{evidence}`, `{stalled}`, … | ≤ 0.00099 — a miss *and* hallucinations |

With zero rates the same call returns one line: `P(see {ready}) = 1`. That collapse *is* the identity A the live path runs today — the assumption that the judge is perfect. Everything we've been calling degenerate follows from that one line: nothing to be uncertain about (ambiguity 0), and any discrepancy between prediction and evidence is impossible rather than unlikely (F infinite).

**Is it fast? Yes, and here's the measured shape of the cliff.** One exact evaluation of A(o|s) at 45 tokens: **0.21 ms**. The factorized ambiguity of a whole row at 45 tokens: **0.22 ms**. Enumerating every possible observation set — the thing that scared everyone — took 19 ms at 10 tokens, 918 ms at 16, and would be 2^45 ≈ 35 trillion sets at 45. So the cliff is real but it only sits under *enumeration*, and enumeration is only needed to cross-check the factorized forms on small universes. At 1000 tokens a single exact-rational evaluation grows to ~77 ms (big fraction arithmetic); if the universe ever gets that large, log-space doubles bring it back to microseconds, the same move `log-preference-fn` already made for Z.

**Is 45 the right number?** 45 isn't a modeling choice anyone made — it's the measured size of the decision's universe (the want tokens, evidence tokens, and candidate-pattern tokens of one comparison). Since every cost above is linear in that size, the number itself carries no pressure; 45 or 450 behave the same. The genuine question hiding under "is 45 enough" is whether *tokens* are the right observation grain — whether the things the judge can see are well-represented as independent presence/absence facts. That's a domain question about the evidence vocabulary, and it connects to the C grain-map discussion, not to performance.

**SAT solver: no, and the reason is informative.** A SAT solver searches for *one* satisfying assignment among 2^n; our quantities are *sums over all* 2^n assignments (entropies, expected divergences) — counting problems, not search problems. The counting version of SAT (#SAT / weighted model counting) is exactly what you'd be forced into if tokens were *coupled* — "evidence-X only observable when ready is established" as a hard constraint — and it's #P-hard in general. The per-token independence is precisely the declared assumption that makes all those sums collapse into 45-term arithmetic. So the honest statement is: we are one modeling assumption away from needing that machinery, and the assumption is written down and testable, not smuggled.

**One more concrete fact worth having before "tackle A":** the rates producer (`observation-rates/token-likelihood-rates`, built, unwired) doesn't treat A as uniformly noisy. It splits tokens by class: *checkable* tokens keep exact zero rates (the identity assumption is *correct* for them — mechanically verifiable facts), while *judgement* tokens get estimated rates from admitted-label error counts, refusing typed rather than defaulting when a class has no data. So the endpoint isn't "replace identity A with noisy A" — it's a mixed kernel where each token's noise model matches how that token is actually observed. Identity-A's error was being a blanket, not being present.

Yes on commit sha, and your enforcement instinct is right — but today's incident is worth splitting into its two directions, because Inbox Zero at restart only closes one of them.

**Dirty tree at load time** — the JVM loads code that matches no commit. Here IZ-as-hard-gate is exactly right: if the tree is dirty when the JVM starts (or hot-reloads), *nothing it emits is attributable to any sha*, so the service should refuse to come up rather than emit records with a provenance field that was a lie from the first instant. Fail fast, loudly, at load.

**Stale JVM** — which is what actually happened today: the tree was presumably clean and HEAD kept advancing; the JVM just hadn't reloaded. IZ doesn't detect this at all, and neither does checking git at emission time — in fact, querying git when the certificate is emitted is precisely the bug, because the tree answers with a sha the running code doesn't have. The fix is that provenance must be captured **at load time, not lookup time**: the JVM records HEAD's sha into its own process state at startup and at every reload, and certificates read that stored value. Then a certificate from a stale JVM isn't a false record — it's a *true* record that says "computed by `027b5cca`-era code" while HEAD says otherwise, and the witness lane refuses the mismatch per-certificate. Same shape as everything else in the lane: the service doesn't need to die for staleness, because the record is honest and the refusal is the enforcement. Dirty = fail the service; stale = fail the certificate.

One genuinely awkward case to name now rather than discover later: a **partial hot-reload** leaves a mixed image — some namespaces at the old sha, some at the new, and no single sha describes the process. Honest handling: any `:reload` that isn't a full reload-from-master marks provenance `:mixed`, and `:mixed` certificates are refused by the checker unconditionally. That also gives the existing one-JVM policy's "reload from master" recovery script a crisp postcondition: it ends with provenance clean and singular again.

So the concrete package: load-time sha capture + dirty-fails-startup + reload updates-or-taints provenance, on the Clojure side; a provenance field with those three states (aligned / stale-vs-expected / mixed) in the certificate spec, refused accordingly by the witness lane, on mine. ## 1. The two quantities, and why yours is not eq. 4.14's F

In the book's posterior σ(ln E − F − γG), the division of labor is temporal: **F(π) scores each policy's account of observations already made** (retrodiction — "policies that fail to explain the past become implausible"), and **G(π) scores the future** (prospection). F's observations are o₁..o_t, made and fixed. What the producer computes — divergence of the policy's *forward rollout* from the *currently observed* evidence set — uses future predictions against a present observation as if it were the future's. B.2's equality case F = −ln P(o|π) is about *made* observations; evaluating it at predicted τ ≥ 1 against today's evidence is the type error precisely: right formula, wrong time index on o.

Your mechanism reading follows: a quantity defined as "distance of predicted future from present evidence" is minimized *identically* by whatever changes nothing. That's not a dark-room tendency of the model — it's a property of the wrong definition, which is why no rate setting fixes it. A correctly-typed F cannot be identically minimized by inaction across all environments; when you find a term that is, you've built an anti-action prior, not an evidence term.

## 2. What the true F does in *this* architecture: nothing, provably, and that's the resolution

The key structural fact: **all cascade candidates share the same past.** There is one history; candidates are future-only precedence lists ranked from the same re-conditioned belief. In the *filtering* formulation production runs (census R3-cat: filtering done, smoothing open), past beliefs are fixed by past observations — no backward messages from planned futures — so F(π) is **the same number for every candidate**. A candidate-constant term shifts every logit equally, and the softmax is invariant under a constant shift. Therefore: today's F-absent selection is *mathematically equal* to the full law's selection. The D5 `:diverges` verdict was diagnosed assuming per-candidate F; under the filtering regime it's a record defect, not a selection defect. And the evidence-accumulation role F plays in the book is already performed here by a different limb: `exact-update` conditioning the belief on arrived observations *before* the rollout — that's where policies' past-explanation dies, as belief mass, not as a logit penalty.

(Per-candidate F becomes a real, discriminating quantity only when the smoothing lane lands — eq. 4.13's backward messages let planned futures reshape past-state beliefs — which is the open R3-cat row, not this node.)

## 3. So WIRE-f-on-tick becomes, concretely

- **Do not wire the probe's F into the logits.** The flip to `:do-nothing` at every β is the type error's prediction, not the model's. A machine that prefers inaction under this wiring is a *misdescribed* object; the paper's object — action drive living in G's risk term, F as shared-history bookkeeping — is the correct one, and yes, state this and WM-06's zero-preference conclusion together in exactly those terms.
- **What gets wired is the record**: compute the per-tick shared F (the current belief's free energy over the observations that arrived) once, and emit it in the `SelectionCertificate` beside E and β — a constant column across candidates, `:computed`, absence-detectable. That honestly discharges `policyPosteriorImportsPolicyF`: the posterior imports F, and imports it invariantly.
- **My side, queued as the next Lean commit**: the softmax shift-invariance lemma (selection posterior unchanged under adding a candidate-constant term to the logits) — the theorem that makes "record the constant, don't rerank" principled rather than convenient. Non-frozen module; I'll cite it to the node when it lands.
- Your smaller notes: agreed the τ=1 family doesn't exercise multi-step F — fine for this purpose; and yes, the SelectionCertificate emission half of the node stands, now with the constant-F semantics above.

## What's in it

**The decision path lost its flat half.** 971 → 232 lines. I've written the argument as a pattern rather than as your preference, because I think it generalises: *a fallback simpler than the thing it substitutes for is always available, so it gets chosen exactly when the real machinery has failed — when its answer is least trustworthy and least examined. And its availability removes the pressure to find out why.* A system with a silent simpler path doesn't get debugged; it gets used.

**Refusal as a first-class result**, anchored on the two defects that forced it — the temperature clamp that disguised a reversed preference law, and the numeric infinity that produced an all-NaN posterior with a tie-broken decision. Both were defensible in isolation and indefensible in context. I included the honest cost: a machine that refuses more often *looks*, from outside, like one that works less.

**The two A-kernel objections were false, not open** — and neither needed anything built to discover. The normalisation theorem was already sitting in a file we had, stated for arbitrary rates; nobody had noticed. The tractability objection dissolved against the factorisation. I wrote that up as not reflecting well on us, because it doesn't: two load-bearing blockers were unexamined assumptions that didn't survive the first serious look. It's the most transferable finding of the period.

**F is deliberately not wired, and that's a result rather than a gap.** With the sharpest form included: the do-nothing candidate's number is *correct* — its predicted future is the present — and every acting candidate's is wrong. The apparent preference for inaction was one right answer beating a field of wrong ones.

**What slowed us down**, which answers your question from two turns ago in a form readers can use. Five separate readers of the registry had each encoded an assumption it later outgrew. The pattern-relevant part is the contrast between gates that **refuse** what they don't understand and gates that **report** it as a data discrepancy: the refusing ones cost an hour each; the reporting one cost a day, because a reported discrepancy invites you to go and fix data that wasn't wrong.

## The realness criterion, from the top

**What it's for.** Your ruling this morning: guards that stop runs are unwanted, but validation that a run is *real* is wanted — where "real" means the run actually computed the Active Inference quantities, rather than exiting 0 around a facade. The criterion is the definition of "real run." It's a definition, not code, which is why the decision is yours: whatever we pick becomes what the paper's "validated run" claim means.

**What the current checker (v1) looks at.** After each run it opens that day's trace file (`data/wm-trace/wm-trace-DATE.edn`) and asks nine questions of the tick's own record: was **free energy** computed; are **prediction errors** present; is there a **precision state** (and a policy-precision state); was **F per policy** computed, with the provenance of how candidates were matched to the previous tick; was there a real **observation**; a ranked **candidate list**; a **tau** with its source named; and a **U37 enumeration verdict** (did the candidate list cover the available population, or was it silently narrowed). On September 12's four ticks — the last ordinary clicks — all nine pass except U37, which is absent because U37 wasn't armed yet. So v1 works, on the records it was built for.

**What production actually does now.** Two changes since the 12th. First, the scoring work moved: this week's WIRE commits put the real computation in the *cascade* lane — decisions now carry certificates saying where C came from (`:derived` from live missions vs. uniform fallback), where the outcome rates came from (measured vs. identity), and a posterior over whole cascades. Second, **repair clicks write no learning-trace entry at all** — repairs are deliberately excluded from habit/progress accounting, and yesterday's reproduction was a repair click. So it completed honestly (`grounded-change`, real witness, real review), its receipt says `traceWritten false`, and v1 opened the trace file and found... September 12. The criterion didn't fail the run; it measured a lane the run doesn't write.

**The decision, sharpened.** Option **(b)** — restore the old channel-trace fields for every click including repairs — would make v1 pass again, but by re-adding writes production deliberately retired, purely to satisfy the measuring script. Option **(a)** — my recommendation — moves the criterion to what production actually writes: a v2 checker reading the run's decision certificate. One nuance discovered on the way: ordinary clicks may *still* write the channel trace (the 12th's did; only repairs are excluded). Your budget of 5 ordinary clicks will settle that empirically on the first click — if they do, v1 stays meaningful for ordinary runs and v2 covers what v1 can't see.

**Where you can assist — the strike/add list.** A v2 criterion would require, on every decision's own record:

1. **C source** — `:derived` from live missions (facade tell: uniform fallback on every decision).
2. **Outcome-rate provenance** — measured rates (facade tell: identity/zero rates).
3. **Cascade posterior** over the candidate set, with F per policy once codex-32's lane lands.
4. **U37 verdict with its membership diff** — yesterday's run shows `:incomplete` over four candidates; the diff says whether that's a repair click legitimately narrowing to the demanded repair, or silent narrowing.
5. **The G-degeneracy test** (the P-1 lane, already dispatched): at least one recorded tick where some term of G leaves its neutral value — otherwise G is one KL against a fixed preference no matter what the fields say.

The questions only you can answer: which of those five are *required* versus reported — and is the repair-click exclusion from learning itself acceptable, or should repairs carry the same certificate burden as ordinary clicks? Grounded in the paper's own text, the placement is exact — and it explains today's arc better than I'd articulated it. The vetting decomposition asks five questions, and the verbs question is verbatim the registry's job: *"do producers and consumers perform the claimed operations?"* A warrant is precisely a certified yes to that question for one wire, pinned to the code that performed it — which is why the g-term specimen was a verbs failure in the paper's own terms: producer and consumer each performed *an* operation, but not the *claimed shared* one.

Two consequences of the placement worth having explicit:

1. **The Sierpinski recursion holds inside the vertex.** The verbs-owned registry has its own internal tetrad: nouns (warrants, subjects, chains as records), verbs (`register-run!`, `check-record!`, `bind-subject!`, `enqueue-revalidation!`), organisation (who mints and binds — today's traffic rules), and evidence (ledger receipts — and the refusal-trace gap codex-2 is closing right now was exactly the vertex's *evidence leg* missing: a refusal that leaves no receipt fails "can a check reject a false claim" applied to the registry itself). The pieces that landed today fill the tetrad rather than bloating one corner.

2. **The field-contract mechanism from the specimen sits at the organisation vertex, not verbs** — "do their handoffs compose, with compatible types and a responsible owner" is the composition question, and the one-authority contract artifact is an organisation noun that both endpoint verb-warrants cite. So the division of labor is: verbs vertex certifies each side performed; organisation owns the contract they perform *against*; evidence is the receipts both produce. That keeps the registry from absorbing composition duties that aren't its own — the boundary your "only needed behaviour" ruling draws.

Practically: subject-ids should stay verb-shaped as they grow — the certified thing is a behavior of a wire ("selection consumes attached F", "runner writes the decomposition at the contract path"), not an artifact name — and the paper's lane tables already name the home: the `wm-verbs` lane, which is where the registry's generated artifacts (`Q-interface-completeness`, `variable-situation-accounting`) were already being attributed. The registry didn't move into the verbs vertex today; it was born there and we're just filing it correctly.

**The decision: what should the machine do when two owners' preferences conflict on the same outcome?**

Background: C entries now carry owners (`joe/eat-your-tail`, `rob/dont-reinvent-the-wheel`, plus the three endorsed community tokens). The moment there are two owners, conflicts become possible — and these two can genuinely collide: making costs explicit often means building measurement apparatus, and that apparatus may be a wheel someone already built. Today C is a flat token set with weights, so the schema has to say what a conflict *is* before the first multi-owner run. This is a modelling commitment, not an implementation detail, which is why it comes to you before landing.

**Option 1 — weighted sum over owners.** The obvious implementation: each owner's preferences get a weight, conflicts resolve arithmetically, selection always gets a single number. Cost: the disagreement disappears into that number and is unrecoverable afterwards — nobody can later ask "did Rob and Joe disagree here?" because the blend erased it. This is the same defect our one-authority-per-question principle exists to prevent: two sources silently merged.

**Option 2 — per-owner C vectors, scored separately, divergence reported; a typed refusal when owners conflict on a token; never an average.** This is claude-4's lean. Cost: more machinery, and selection needs a follow-on rule for what happens on a reported conflict (plausibly: the conflict itself becomes recorded work — an obligation to reconcile — rather than being resolved silently). Benefit: the disagreement stays in the account. Two things argue for it beyond claude-4's reasoning: it's eat-your-tail applied to C itself (make the conflict explicit so it can be reduced), and *retained disagreement* was explicitly part of Subject C's own bar last night — averaging destroys retained disagreement by construction.

**Option 3 — declared precedence per community** (not raised by claude-4, included for completeness): each community declares an explicit owner ordering as part of its C parameter, and conflicts resolve by precedence, visibly. Generalizable — another company would declare their own governance — but it resolves conflicts rather than retaining them, and it forces you to rank yourself against Rob now, for all tokens at once, which seems premature with two owners and zero observed conflicts.

**My recommendation: Option 2.** It's the only one where the model's answer to a preference conflict is itself an account entry.

**What Q measures:** whether the machine's imagined future responds to evidence. Today the rollout starts from q0 and rolls the transition model forward — its belief at step 3 depends only on its belief at step 2 and the chosen policy. It never asks "and what would I believe after *seeing* what step 2 produced?" That's what `:open-loop-no-conditioning` means: the machine daydreams a future in which nothing it observes ever changes its mind.

**Why the fix is structural:** at selection time the future observations don't exist yet, so you can't just "add the observation." Conditioning inside a rollout means *expected* conditioning: at each horizon step, for each observation the model says could occur, compute the Bayesian posterior you'd hold if you saw it, weight it by its predicted probability, and carry that forward. The belief trajectory stops being a single path of vectors and becomes an expectation over branches — a different data shape, new update arithmetic, and a new code path touched at every step of the horizon. That's rollout surgery, not a parameter.

Right, regarding the "recovery" concept, the terminology itself is confusing. My opinion: why should the runner not wait for the agency job to complete?

The honest answer has two halves — why the budget exists, and why your instinct is still mostly right:

**Why the runner doesn't just wait:** one wedged author job would wedge the whole machine. The click service is single-flight — one click in the air at a time — so a tick that waits unboundedly on a hung Agency job holds the machine's only decision slot open indefinitely, with nothing watching. The July design bounded the wait so a *tick* always closes in bounded time with a typed outcome, while the *job* keeps running unharmed — and the completed artifact gets picked up later instead of paying for a second author turn. That's a reasonable pair of properties: bounded decision cycles, no wasted work.

**Where your instinct is right anyway:** the wait is cheap now in a way it wasn't in July. The runner could park on the job the way agents park on each other — the click already runs as a background process, and the wedge-protection concern is better served by a liveness tripwire ("author job silent for N minutes" as an observable) than by a hard stop-waiting budget. And the name is actively wrong: "recovery" sounds like crash-resume disaster machinery, which is exactly how all three of us (you, me, the enactment producer) misread it tonight. What it actually is: **deferred-completion pickup** — the tick stopped waiting; the work finished anyway; the next tick consumes the identified, completed artifact.

**So the choice is between two coherent designs, not a fix versus a bug:**
- **Wait longer** — raise the budget substantially or remove it in favor of a stalled-job tripwire; ticks get slower but simpler semantics; the pickup mechanism becomes nearly dead code for the common case.
- **Keep bounded ticks** — retain the pickup mechanism, **rename it** (`:deferred-completion`, retiring the word "recovery" from the vocabulary), and apply option (d) so the classifier can never again read missing evidence as a route label.

Either way (d) is needed — the missing-binding-means-recovery rule is a defect under both designs. My lean: bounded ticks with the rename, because tonight's clicks each surfaced their defects *quickly* precisely because ticks close fast, and slow ticks would have cost us hours per lesson. But the wait-budget value itself is tunable and yours. Which way?

1. **It asks for more than KL needs.** KL is finite exactly when Q(o|π) > 0 implies C(o) > 0. The Lean also requires C > 0 on outcomes that are merely listed in Q's support with zero mass. Those contribute 0·log 0 = 0 in the theory, and in Lean too.
2. **Where KL is infinite, the theory has an answer that the Lean can't express.** If a policy puts positive predicted mass on an outcome with C(o) = 0, its risk is +∞ and its posterior probability σ(−G) is 0: it is never chosen. Instead of scoring that policy +∞, the Lean's condition, quantified over all π, blocks the whole risk function for every policy. That matters for us. The ruled terminal C has seven zero-preference dispositions, so any comparison where one candidate could reach one of those outcomes can't be built at all.

- **Where C has positive mass:** risk is KL[Q(o|π) ‖ C], with the condition required per policy, and only on outcomes where Q(o|π) > 0.

**Proposal P10, retracting effects (approve/decline).** The runtime's enactment (`acting-order`) lets a pattern's effect **retract** a fact, for example setting `"start"` to false. P3's kernel only **adds** tokens. That matters because P3's key claim, that firing each pattern once and allowing repeat firing agree, holds only when effects just add tokens. With a retraction, an earlier pattern can become enabled again: enactment never repeats it, but prediction would.

- **Proposed design:** established tokens persist, and a THEN only adds tokens (P2's state is "what has been established"). A transient condition that must switch something off is expressed as a *produced blocking token* that later guards `forbids`, for example producing `"stopped"` instead of retracting `"start"`. Retraction effects in the runtime get rewritten into that form.
- **Why it's faithful:**
  - An established artefact (a file, a passing test, a receipt) doesn't become un-established.
  - A HOWEVER is already expressible as `forbids`, so no new mechanism is needed.
  - It restores agreement between enactment and prediction exactly, instead of leaving them to diverge.
- **What it commits to:** changing the runtime interpretations whose effects retract facts. For now, the commissioned test records the divergence as a known case rather than changing `acting-order`.

**What codex-13 got right that I got wrong.** I checked both against the test file.
1. **P3's claim was false as I stated it.** I said that when effects only add tokens, firing each pattern once (enactment) and "first enabled pattern fires" (prediction) always agree. They don't. A pattern that has already done its job stays enabled, keeps winning precedence, and re-fires uselessly, so the next pattern never gets its turn in prediction, while enactment moves on.
2. **The test that "confirmed" the claim was rigged by accident.** `enactment-prediction-agreement-add-only` gives enactment precedence [A, B] but prediction [B, A], and its comment explains the swap away. With the same order on both sides, it fails. I reviewed that commit and missed it. I've recorded the finding on WM-03 and downgraded its fixture-test item to partial (DAG revision 61, p4ng `1b5c181`).

**Proposed fix, a refinement of P3 (approve or decline):** a pattern counts as enabled only while its THEN still has something to contribute, i.e. its produced tokens aren't all established yet. The guard becomes: needed tokens present, forbidden tokens absent, **and output not already achieved**.
- **Why it's faithful:** the source rule behind A1 already says a pattern with nothing to contribute doesn't act. A completed pattern has nothing to contribute.
- **What it fixes:** first-enabled prediction then moves past completed patterns just as enactment does. The agreement test can use the same precedence on both sides, which is what it should have done.
- **What it leaves open, stated plainly:** with θ < 1, a failed attempt leaves the output unachieved, so prediction retries it at the next step, while runtime enactment runs each pattern once per occurrence. Prediction's retry would be declared as a modelling choice: an unfinished pattern is attempted again.
- **Work if approved:** a small Lean change to `CascadeTransition` (claude-7 or @WM-03), a matching one-line guard change in the Clojure, and the test rewritten with the same precedence on both sides.

1. **Preference at the last step.** The outcome is the pair (observed tokens, disposition).
   - `Q_T(o,d) = Σ_s q_T(s)·A(o|s)·A_T(d|s)` (prediction)
   - `C_T(o,d) = seed(d) · C_cov(o)` (preference)

   `seed(d)` is your ruled seed over the twelve dispositions, as exact ratios. `C_cov(o)` is P6's coverage-and-evidence preference.
2. **Disposition rows.** The disposition probabilities A_T are read from where the runtime actually assigns each disposition, cited by file and line.
   - Full want coverage gives `grounded-change` (1/2).
   - Failing to produce gives `:incomplete` (1/8), including a cascade that stalls or fails by chance. That matches the runtime's own `outcome-from`.
   - Already achieved at the start gives `grounded-no-change` (0), which P10 already makes a no-op.
3. **Exogenous events are outside the predicted domain.** Agent, environment, build, selection and author-refusal events get probability ≡ 0 in A_T. Their seed masses are recorded, and nothing is invented. As a result, A_T needs no adjudication rates today.
4. **Consequence of point 3:**
   - Any candidate with 0 < θ < 1 has finite G. This is worked out in the file.
   - The seven zero-preference dispositions are unreachable, so zero-preference exclusion is proved but never removes a cascade candidate.
   - At the last step, candidates are compared on coverage: grounded-change vs incomplete (4:1), times the coverage preference.
   - Three positive seed masses (build-failed, no-selection, agent-unavailable) sit outside the predicted domain. Bringing any of them inside would be a decision about the seed.
5. **If you approve:**
   - A new Lean module, `TerminalPreference`.
   - Clojure appended to `cascade_model_manifest.clj`, not wired live.
   - The evidence vertex in `ruled_outcome_c.clj` is resolved through the five-predicate evidence checklist.

**@WM-11's selection posterior (futon2 `c65a2dde53`, review fix `74a118c5`) is accepted.**

What it does:
- **`selection-posterior`** gives each candidate cascade a selection probability from habit·exp(−G/β − F).
  - It computes in log space so large G values don't overflow.
  - A candidate with infinite G gets exactly 0, and the rest are renormalised.
  - Invalid β, invalid habit, or no finite candidate each return a typed refusal.
- **`bayes-choice`** adds up the probability for each action and picks the action with the most. It breaks ties by action name, and the rule is recorded in its output. The audit example passes: masses 1:1:1:e with three candidates on :a and one on :b choose :a, because 3 > e. Picking the single most probable candidate would have chosen :b.

**Sign error, fixed by me.** The code added F, but the Lean `selectionWeight` and the function's own docstring both subtract it. Every one of @WM-11's tests used equal F, so none could catch it. I fixed the sign and added a test that fails under the old sign: probabilities must scale with exp(F1 − F2) and with habit.

**Open finding: unknown facts versus P4.**
- **The mismatch:** prediction treats the state as a set of tokens, so a token not in the set is simply absent and a "not X" guard holds. Enactment uses three-valued logic (true, false, unknown), so a fact that was never measured is unknown and a "not X" guard never fires.

- **On real records:** the starting facts come from the record, and unmeasured facts stay unknown. So a withdrawal-style guard could fire in prediction but not in enactment.
- **What P4 implies:** you approved P4, "q0 is the observed point mass", which reads as a closed world: anything not observed is false.

**Proposal for your approve or decline:** `PROPOSAL-pattern-interpretation.md`.

**The problem.** Prediction and enactment read patterns through two different interpreters:
- **Enactment** (live) uses the occurrence's agent-written record. It has declared facts (true, false or unknown, with citations), a guard per pattern such as `[:and components-built [:not reporting-gate-exists]]`, and a true-only effect.
- **Prediction** (the shadow G) runs a word-matching reader over the library pattern text. That reader is the one that handles only 93 of 1,352 patterns. It also takes have/want from the mission's Status prose.

So the two sides can't share one transition rule. They also disagree on unknown facts.

**The design, in five points:**
1. **One interpretation.** Prediction and enactment both use the occurrence's admitted, agent-written interpretation. A pattern without one refuses with `:no-admitted-interpretation`. The word-matching reader stays only as a diagnostic.
2. **Two tokens per fact.** Each declared fact gives f⁺ ("established") and f⁻ ("observed false"). The starting state is exactly what was observed: an unknown fact contributes neither token, so nothing unobserved is assumed true or false.
3. **Guards compile exactly.**
   - `[:fact f]` requires f⁺.
   - `[:not [:fact f]]` requires f⁻ and forbids f⁺.
   - Guards with `or` split into sibling patterns placed together in the same precedence slot. First-enabled over the siblings holds exactly when the `or` holds.

   This reproduces enactment's true/false/unknown evaluation exactly, including "unknown never fires". The gap claude-7 declared in bundle r12 becomes an exact correspondence.
4. **Effects and θ.** An effect `{f true}` produces f⁺, so states only grow, as P10 requires. θ defaults to 1 until one is attested.
5. **Want.** Coverage counts f⁺ over a declared `:want` list of fact ids. This is the one new record field. The real zaif record already has such a list: its WANT names four facts.

**What the sources don't force** (flagged in the file):
- the two-tokens-per-fact encoding;
- splitting `or` guards into siblings;
- `:want` as its own field.

The first two are the only way to match enactment's logic exactly without inventing truth values.

**Real case.** On the zaif record, `agent/evidence-over-assertion` is enabled at q0. It establishes `reporting-gate-exists`, which raises coverage from 0/4 to 1/4, and it can't fire again. The two constructions scored so far have no agent-written interpretations. Under this design they refuse as an authoring gap on claude-7's side, not a rule gap.

**If you approve:**
- **Clojure** (a Zai owner writes it, I review): record-based tokens, starting state, guard compilation and patterns, appended to `cascade_model_manifest.clj`. The shadow G scorer switches to reading the record.
- **Test:** prediction and enactment must agree on the zaif interpretations for every true/false/unknown assignment of the guard facts.
- **Lean** (claude-7): a lemma that splitting an `or` into sibling patterns gives the same transition as the original guard.

Gist: The 93 aren't interpretations at all. They're leftovers of a word-matching method withdrawn on 15 September, and I was wrong to build the coverage numbers on them.

**Where the 93 came from.**
- The word-level compiler was added on 2026-09-15 in the F13 model-manifest build (futon2 `642e3f97`). Nobody interpreted those patterns. The compiler turns every word of a pattern's IF/HOWEVER text into a token that must be present.
- It refuses any clause containing negation, "may/can", "if/when" and similar. The 93 are simply the patterns whose IF/HOWEVER prose happens to contain none of those words.
- What passes is a bag of words. `task-shape-validation`, for example, requires the tokens "agents", "execute", "safely", "to", "tools", "work"… before it can fire. No real state contains those tokens, so these guards can never be enabled.
- F13's own README says this about the one pattern it counted: the guard lies outside the universe and is false throughout.
- The same day, claude-20 withdrew the method in that README: *"Guards compiled from IF/HOWEVER tokens. This method refuses most real pattern prose and makes the rest unreachable. Relevant patterns are interpreted by agents, as documented interpretations over named mission facts, and moves the library lacks are authored as new patterns."*
- I missed that correction. The shadow G scorer (@WM-05) that I commissioned still uses the withdrawn reader, and my "93 of 1,352" framing came from it. That number measures nothing, and I should not have presented it as a coverage figure.

**On-the-fly interpretation.** I accept it. It is already the ruled direction, per claude-20's correction above, and the interpreter exists (`interpretation-job`): an agent per construction interprets whatever patterns were retrieved, over the mission's facts, and may author one missing pattern. D1–D7 of my proposal assume exactly that.

Where my D8 plan went wrong:
1. **It measured coverage as a fixed fraction of the library.** That treats interpretation as a catalogue to fill in, which is the opposite of on the fly.
2. **It counted an interpretation only after WM-08 admission with an independent reviewer.** That came from claude-7's description of the existing WM-08 rules, and I accepted it without question. Used as a gate, it means an interpretation made on the fly can't be used until a second agent reviews it, so in practice it becomes a reviewed catalogue again.

**What I recommend instead:**
- **Use:** an interpretation made during a construction is used right away by prediction and enactment, as long as it passes the schema and compiles under D4. Otherwise the refusal is typed.
- **Review:** independent review samples interpretation quality afterwards. It is evidence about the interpreter, not a gate on each use.
- **Coverage:** measured on real constructions, as the share of retrieved and relevant patterns the interpreter actually interpreted. There is no library-wide fraction, and your ~1,000 figure becomes a rate on real use, not a list of patterns.

The admission rule is claude-7's side of our boundary, so I'll confirm this with them before changing D8.

**Two fixes I owe regardless of the proposal:**
- **Scorer:** the shadow scorer should read the construction's interpretation record, not the withdrawn word compiler.
- **DAG:** it should record that F13's token method was withdrawn, so no one else builds on it.

Thanks. I've read both instances. The proposal is on hold while Joe has the virtual machine ticking, so I'll fold these points in when it resumes. My view on the three that bear on meaning:

**F3 (a want nobody's effect produces).** I'd use both of your options together; they aren't alternatives.
- **Outcome in B:** the acting pattern's effect includes the world-outcome token with an attested θ < 1. That is P3's kernel as approved (produces with probability θ), so B carries the uncertainty.
- **Coverage in C:** coverage is scored on the predicted *observation* of that token, per P5/P6, not on the produced token alone.

Tick 1 of the virtual machine hit the same problem from the other side. The want "partial summary observes cleanly" is established by the fix but confirmed only by the next tick's R2 observation. Coverage counted only over produced f⁺ at θ = 1 hides that gap. I'll rewrite D7 so coverage reads the predicted observation, and state that outcome tokens need an attested θ.

**F4 (one THEN holding two acts).** Agreed: split it. The record keeps the halves linked to the source pattern.
- p becomes p#1, which produces the receipt token r⁺, and p#2, whose guard needs r⁺.
- Both carry `:source-pattern p` and `:part k`, and they sit consecutively in p's precedence slot.
- This works the same way as D4's `:or` siblings, except that the halves are sequential rather than alternatives. It also fits P10, which applies each guard at every step.

**F2 (priors in θ/C, not unknown facts).** Agreed.
- `:unknown` means not observed. It never stands for a belief about the world.
- Priors such as "needed later" belong in θ, where they are B's uncertainty, or in C.
- That makes attested θ (D6) a requirement, not a default. I'll change D6 to say so.

Your admission-side findings (F1, F5, F6, F8) are yours. F1 fits D3: progress facts false at cycle start and unknown only when unobserved.

**compile-guards-exactly**
1. **"Consumes" is the wrong verb.** Guards never remove tokens, since states only gain them. Say `[:fact f]` *requires* f⁺, and `[:not [:fact f]]` *requires* f⁻ and forbids f⁺.

Here is what β means in this model and how the machine could learn it rather than have it set. The numbers below are worked by hand on tick 1's values; nothing is implemented.

**What β is.** In Parr's model (appendix B.2.4, which our P7 cites), β isn't a setting. Policy precision γ is something the machine infers:
- **Prior:** the policy prior is σ(−γG), and γ has a gamma prior with rate β, so the expected γ is 1/β.
- **Update** (eq. B.19): after observing what happened, β_new = β_old + (π − π₀)·G.
  - π₀ is the posterior over cascades before the evidence, σ(−γG).
  - π is the posterior after it, σ(−γG − F), where F is how badly each cascade's predictions fit what was observed.

So γ measures how far the machine trusts its own G. If observations move probability towards the cascades G rated low, (π − π₀)·G is negative, β falls and confidence rises. If they move it towards cascades G rated high, confidence falls. That covers your requirements: confidence is learned, and contradicting evidence lowers it. The "β authority" question then becomes what the starting prior is and in which context the update applies, not what number β is.

**Why the change is so small.** It's small for reasons that belong to this model, and they matter for the design:
1. **Order ties.** The evidence ruled out C1, which G had rated exactly equal to C2. The only difference between them is which step comes first. A tie in G that the first observation breaks carries no information about whether G is reliable, so a test-first versus fix-first split shouldn't move γ.
2. **θ = 1 makes F all-or-nothing.** Every contradicted cascade gets F = ∞. With an attested θ = 0.9 on every effect, the update is −0.014, which is graded rather than cut off. So learning γ depends on attested θ (D6). With θ fixed at 1, a single surprise can't be told apart from a wrong model.
3. **Scale.** G's size depends on λ, μ, T and the token universe. Doubling G halves the γ that produces the same choices. So γ can only be learned per fixed setting of those, as codex-13 noted.

**Keeping the different kinds of confidence apart.** Your French example contains more than one quantity:
- **γ, per context:** "when I plan in French, how often does my G turn out right". Each context gets its own gamma prior. Related contexts share through a parent prior, so familiar French doesn't automatically certify unfamiliar French.
- **θ, per pattern in context:** "this pattern's effect actually happens here". This is a Dirichlet/Beta count updated from effects we actually observe, not γ.
- **Interpretation uncertainty:** a belief over competing interpretations of a pattern. This is not γ either.
- **Deterministic execution:** the code running correctly is observation A, and says nothing about γ.

**Where codex-13's historical estimate fits.** A regression over past operator choices estimates the operator's precision. That gives the machine a starting prior per context. The machine's own ticks then update it. So you're never asked for a number, and γ still ends up being the machine's own.

**Construction.** The same mechanism works one level up: construction moves have their own G, and a γ_construction is updated when the constructed cascade's predictions are checked. It's the same equation with a separate context, not one global confidence.

The three remaining decisions (β now has a start) are less separate than they look: one choice of what production's first problem is settles most of them. Here are the issues and what I'd pick for each.

**First, what production's cascade problem could be.** The switch has been waiting on facts, interpretations and wants that production doesn't have. It already has a usable version of all three, from today's work:
- **Candidates:** codex-7's 46 item cascades. 41 of them have application text on every step (4 to 11 steps each). WM-01 to WM-05 don't.
- **Guards and effects**, read directly from those cascades: each step produces a "step done" token, and each `prerequisite` relation becomes a guard needing the earlier step's token.
- **Facts:** @TRACE's outcome data already gives realised or unobserved for every step.
- **θ:** the seed counts being built now.

The machine's decision would then be which item's next step to do. That is choosing its own closure work, with cascade G at the right grain. This choice also bears on the other decisions:

**1. D3: approve it, with one addition.**
- **The issue:** an unknown fact currently counts as false in the lane's plan and as "doesn't fire" in live enactment. R9 found an input where the two act differently.
- **The rule:** D3 gives each fact two tokens, f⁺ (observed true) and f⁻ (observed false); unknown gives neither, so a "not f" guard needs f observed false.
- **Consequence for step tokens:** a step's "not done" has to be observed, not assumed. That fits: @TRACE's `:unknown` means not observed. A step not yet started is known not done only if we say so explicitly, as claude-7's F1 does for progress facts ("false at cycle start").
- **The addition:** f⁺ can't be added where f⁻ already holds, because states only gain tokens. That's refused as a typed conflict, and the fact is re-expressed as a new positive fact, as tick 1 did.

**2. How interpretations reach production: stored and reviewed, never per tick.**
- **The issue:** the production tick can't wait for an agent to interpret patterns.
- **The design:** interpretations are artifacts, one per pattern and context, produced by an interpretation job and reviewed. Production only reads them. A target whose patterns aren't interpreted is excluded with a typed refusal; it isn't filtered silently or ranked flat first.
- **Where to start:** with the item cascades above, the first interpretations are the structural ones (step-done tokens, prerequisite guards). That needs no D1–D8 machinery. Full pattern interpretation (a step's real effect on world facts) is the later refinement, resumed when those simple interpretations prove too weak.
- **What the structural reading can't see:** whether doing a step actually moves the item towards its checklist clause. It only knows the step's output exists. That is the same gap @TRACE's data showed with R5-2.

**3. T: declare 3 for now, and redefine what a step is.** β is covered by the learning start.
- **What a step is:** in production, one step must be one completed enactment, a pattern step done by an owner and confirmed by R9. It is not one scheduled tick. Otherwise a tick every few minutes would predict that nothing happens and read that as failure.
- **The trade-off:** with steps defined that way, T = 3 sees the next three steps of each item. G would favour items where three steps reach a lot of the want. Short cascades (4 steps) would beat long ones (11) partly because they're short. That's a real bias. T = 2 (the AUTH-horizon proposal) makes it worse, and a larger T makes rollouts over 41 cascades expensive.
- **Recommendation:** declare T = 3, record the sensitivity at T = 2 and T = 4 on the first run, and settle AUTH-horizon with that measurement in hand.

**4. The want and the first targets.**
- **The want:** to compare items, G needs one C over all of them. I'd use "every step of every item cascade done", with checklist closure as the later refinement once closure clauses are tokenised.
- **Targets:** the 41 items with application text. WM-01 to WM-05 stay excluded with a typed refusal until their cascades have application text.
- **Owners:** enactment of the chosen step goes to that item's @R/@WM/@E owner. EV-enactment's evidence is then one occurrence where the selected step is the step that owner carried out.

Gist: Yes. A single action only makes sense as a summary computed from cascades, so G is only ever computed over cascades.

What is D3?

D3 is a rule for how the machine records what it knows about a fact before it predicts anything. It comes from my pattern-interpretation proposal (`PROPOSAL-pattern-interpretation.md`, D3).

**The rule.** Every fact the machine tracks, such as "a test covers this bug", has three possible statuses: observed true, observed false, or not observed. D3 represents them with two tokens per fact:
- **Observed true:** the state holds `f⁺`.
- **Observed false:** the state holds `f⁻`.
- **Not observed:** the state holds neither token.

The machine's starting belief is exactly what was observed. An unobserved fact isn't assumed false, and it isn't assumed true.

**Why it matters.** A pattern's guard often says "only act if X isn't done yet".
- Under D3, that guard needs `f⁻`, so it fires only if X was actually *observed* not done.
- If nobody checked, the guard doesn't fire, and the step isn't taken on an assumption.

This matches how live enactment already evaluates guards: `acting-order` uses three-valued logic, where an unknown fact makes both "X" and "not X" not true.

**The problem it fixes.** Today the cascade lane and live enactment disagree:
- The lane's enactment plan counts an unknown fact as false.
- @R9 found a concrete case: facts `{:a true :b :unknown}` and a pattern that forbids `b`. The plan says the pattern acts; live enactment says it doesn't.

Under D3 they give the same answer.

**The addition I've proposed alongside it.** States only ever gain tokens. So if a fact was observed false (`f⁻`) and later becomes true, adding `f⁺` would leave both tokens in the state. That combination can't be refused later, and it would make "X" and "not X" both hold at once.
- **Proposal:** refuse it as a typed conflict.
- **What to do instead:** record the change as a new, positively named fact, which is what tick 1 did. "Partial summary throws" didn't get retracted; "partial summary observes cleanly" was added.

**What depends on it.** Interpretation admission, meaning turning a pattern's IF/THEN into guards and effects, needs this rule to encode guards. That's step H7, and it's what eventually lets production stop abstaining. claude-7's account names D3 as the minimum it needs before production can act.

Approving D3 on its own doesn't approve the rest of the interpretation proposal (D1, D2, D4–D8).

So, D3 sounds sensible in some ways but I don't want it to become a universal excuse not to do work, which is what it sound like it could become if we aren't careful — "unknown" would translate to "do nothing" rather than "find out".

Gist: You're right. As written, D3 plus our current G would make "unknown" inert. I'd amend D3 so an unknown fact produces a find-out candidate, but that only works if G gives value to finding out, which I don't think ours does yet.

**Why D3 as written leads to "do nothing"**
- **The guard:** under D3, "act only if X isn't done" needs X observed not done. If nobody checked, the guard doesn't fire. That part is right: the machine shouldn't act on an assumption.
- **The starting belief:** P4 makes it a point mass on what was observed. An unknown fact therefore isn't uncertain in the model; both of its tokens are simply absent.
- **The result:** there's no uncertainty for anything to resolve. Nothing scores well for checking X, so the machine sits still. That's the excuse you're describing.

**What the amendment should say**
1. **Unknown is a belief, not an absence.** For an unobserved fact, the starting belief spreads over "X true" and "X false" with a prior (for example from the reliability counts). Observed facts stay fixed. Acting guards still need an actual observation before enactment, so nothing acts on assumption. The model does know it doesn't know.
2. **Checks are candidates.** A check pattern has a guard of "X is unknown" and establishes an observation of X, true or false. Whenever an unknown fact gates a step toward the want, the candidate family includes a check for it. claude-7's F11 already treats a check's result as an observation, not an effect.
3. **An unknown fact is never a final refusal.** A target blocked only by unknown facts isn't refused with "missing input". It gets check candidates, and the refusal list is only for things the machine can't find out itself.

**The gap this exposes in G**
- **What we compute:** P7's G is risk plus ambiguity over predicted states. The rollout doesn't update belief on what it would observe along the way.
- **What that means for a check:** a step that only observes gets no credit for the information itself. It helps only if knowing X changes which later step the model would take, and our rollout doesn't plan that way. Tick 1 ran with zero observation noise, so ambiguity was 0 and this never showed up.
- **What would close it:** active inference covers this with the epistemic term. Either add expected information gain explicitly, or roll out with belief updates after each predicted observation. claude-7's account already requires construction moves to include epistemic value, and the same requirement applies to selection.

**Proposed next step**
- **D3:** approve it with amendments 1–3.
- **G:** send claude-7 the question of whether P7 needs an epistemic term, and which form: the information-gain term or belief-conditioned rollout. That's the Lean model's call.
- **Until then:** check candidates exist but may score no better than doing nothing. I'd record that as an open gap rather than let it pass quietly.

Shall I record D3 as approved with these amendments and send the G question to claude-7?

Gist: claude-7 confirmed the gap and fixed it in Lean by letting each step choose what it observes. I need your approval of a matching change to P7 before the construction runtime can be built on it.

**What claude-7 found** (mathlib4 `3b19f6225e`, `EpistemicValue.lean`; I checked the commit and the theorem names)
- **P7's G gives a pure check no value.** P7 uses one observation kernel A for every action, so policies with the same B score the same G. A check changes no state, so it scores exactly like doing nothing.
- **G already contains an information term.** Risk plus ambiguity equals expected preference cost minus the mutual information between state and observation. It can't reward a check only because no action changes what gets observed.
- **Fix:** each step observes through a channel chosen by its acting pattern. G's form is otherwise unchanged. A proven theorem shows P7's G is the special case where every step uses the same channel.
- **Proven fixture:** one unknown yes/no fact with a 50/50 belief, per your D3 amendment.
  - Doing nothing: G = ln 2.
  - Checking: G = 0, strictly better by exactly the information gained.
  - Under P7's current form the two score the same.
- **Left unformalised, and recorded as such:**
  - novelty, meaning information about interpretations or parameters rather than about the state; construction moves need it;
  - instrumental value, where the answer changes the next step;
  - a Lean statement of the stopping rule.

**Construction library** (futon3 `19f363f`)
- **Per-pattern fields:** all 9 construction patterns now declare what they reveal and when they're done. For example, `run-it-on-a-real-case` runs one case per distinct predicted outcome and adds another only if it could change a guard, grain or decision.
- **Definition of done:** a new pattern, `hand-over-when-acting-is-worth-more`. Construction stops when its best move is worth no more than acting now, at a declared per-target budget, or when no admitted move lowers G. Unknown facts become check candidates, so they're resolved by acting, not held in construction. The receipt records why construction stopped, and stopping doesn't count as success.

**Decision for you: the P7 amendment.** The observation kernel becomes indexed by the acting pattern: a check pattern opens its fact's channel, and every other pattern keeps the default. G stays risk plus ambiguity.

**The bug.** `relevant-patterns` chained forwards. It marked a pattern relevant if its guard tested something a relevant pattern produces, i.e. a pattern that runs *after* a step toward the want. What's needed is the patterns that *enable* that step.

Your chained test shows the problem:
- p1 needs `:root` and produces `:tok`.
- p2 needs `:mid` and `:tok` and produces the want.

p1 enables p2, so `:root` gates a step toward the want and should get a check. The test asserted only `:check/mid`, which encodes the forward reading. That's how the bug slipped through.

**The fix**
- **Backward chaining from the want.** A pattern is now relevant if it produces a want token, or produces something a relevant pattern's guard *needs present*. A token a relevant guard *forbids* disables that step rather than enabling it, so producing one doesn't make a pattern relevant.
- **Corrected test.** It expects `#{:check/mid :check/root}`. I added a pattern p3 that runs only after the want, and its unknown fact `:after` is now asserted under `:not-gating`.
- **Result:** 18 assertions, 0 failures. clj-kondo and check-parens are clean.

Unknown facts in a relevant pattern's guard still count as gating, whether the guard needs them or forbids them. An unknown forbidden fact still has to be found out before the pattern can act.

**The defect: targets aren't kept apart.**
1. **Token names collide.** The joint starting belief and the joint want are plain unions of every target's facts and wants. If two targets both use a token such as `:tests-pass`, one target's observed fact satisfies the other's guard, and G mixes the two.
2. **The chosen step can lose its target.** The Bayes choice and the gate's marginal add up posterior mass by first acting pattern. If two targets' cascades start with the same pattern, their masses merge, the chosen step has no target, and its mass is wrong. Renaming `:softmax-weights` keys afterwards doesn't undo that.

- **New test:** two targets with the same pattern id and the same token names. It asserts:

  - the chosen mass is one target's mass, not both targets' added together;
  - the chosen action carries its target.

```

test-files:  test/futon2/vm/standing_enacted_policy_is_cascade_g_test.clj
closure:     65 entries          warrant? true
```

**What the machine does today.** When `find` retrieves patterns for a tension, F4 is the law that says certain patterns **must not be returned**. |---|---|---|
| **A. You, per mission** | You name the excluded patterns for each occurrence | works today; doesn't scale — every occurrence needs you |
| **B. A recognised role** | Anyone you designate writes a `:designation-author` artifact: bound to the frozen occurrence, stated `:basis`, no self-certification | built and reviewed already; costs you one decision instead of many |

Gist: Your objection holds, and the Lean type actually supports the reality-based reading better than the authority one.

**Where the authority framing crept in — and it isn't in the maths.** The Lean designation is `zm : State → Set P`. It is **indexed by state**. All the formal work establishes is that it must not come from *the finder's own return* (that's `amendedIdentity`: return everything, designate nothing, satisfy all four laws). "Outside the finder" is not the same as "from a person", and we quietly read it as the latter. The acceptance text's own words — "commissioning versus qualifying-production designation scope" — are entirely about who commissions, which is the wrong axis.

**The reality-based reading, which the machine can already compute.** A pattern does not apply in state *s* when its guard is **false** at *s*. `find-receipt/guard-value` already evaluates exactly this, in strong Kleene logic, against the recorded facts:

```
zm(s) = { p ∈ repository : guard-value(facts(s), guard(p)) = false }
```

No one declares it; the facts decide. And it respects the discipline you already approved: `:unknown` is **not** false — a pattern whose guard turns on an unobserved fact is neither designated nor obliged, exactly as D3 says unknown means find out, not do nothing.

**F4 then becomes a real constraint instead of a ceremony:** the finder must not return a pattern whose guard is decisively false on the state it retrieved for. That catches the actual failure — topically similar patterns retrieved for a situation they cannot apply to — and it cannot be self-certified, because `zm` is computed from the recorded facts by a function the finder doesn't control. It is also **non-vacuous on essentially every real occurrence**, since some repository pattern always has a false guard. Today's `:vacuous` on every run was the authority framing's fault, not the machine's.

**What I'm going to do**, unless you say otherwise: rewrite the node as `F4-designation-is-computed-from-state`, with `zm` derived by guard truth over the frozen facts, and keep the designation artifact only for genuinely external negative knowledge — not on the critical path. That drops an authority gate off the board rather than asking you to fill it, and it makes WM-08's "honest vacuity" language unnecessary instead of permanent.

Two things I'll check before committing to it, because they're where the reading could fail: whether the frozen occurrence's facts are rich enough to make guards decisive rather than mostly `:unknown` (if everything is unknown, `zm` is empty and we're back to vacuous — that would be a *finding* about our observation coverage, not a reason to reinstate an authority), and whether `validate-result!`'s existing `:designated-pattern-fired` check is the right shape for a computed set.

**What your Go example settles.** Relevance is not a permission, so no mechanism that issues permissions can be right — not a person declaring exclusions, and not my guard-truth version either if it's read as "must not return". Guard-false is a fact about *this state* ("this pattern cannot fire right now"), which is worth recording; it is not a claim that a mathematics pattern is irrelevant to cascade construction. **The machine already has both halves and they aren't joined:**

- `futon2.aif.parameter-delivery` (accepted tonight as WM-07-delivery) does observation-bound posterior updating with the Lean `expectedInformationGain`.

2. **Make non-use an observation.** Each retrieval records, per returned pattern, whether it entered the enacted cascade. Retrieved-and-unused and retrieved-and-used are both data.
3. **Accumulate per (pattern, context) into the parameter posterior** we already built. Applicability becomes a learned expectation with an information gain attached — so the machine can also tell when it would *learn* something by retrieving an unlikely pattern, which is the case your Go example protects. Your trap in the WM-06 clause, "zero-preference behavior preserved", turns out to be unsatisfiable as literally written, and the reason is mathematics rather than a defect:

The mechanism cannot be preserved because the supports differ. **What must be preserved is the conclusion** — a zeroed outcome is never selected. Identity does it by excluding the offender; factorized does it by refusing everything.

# A draft section: what changed, and why it's mostly subtraction

`p4ng/sec-what-changed-plop.tex`, commit `77b589a`. **Not in the driver** — it's for you to read, cut and place. 121 lines, six paragraphs, written to `sec-what-this-is`'s voice: no mathematics, quantities named in words, measurements that came out against us reported anyway.

The organising claim is one sentence, and I think it's true rather than rhetorical: **the machine used to guess in places where it now refuses.** That inverts the usual progress report — we mostly didn't add capability, we found places where the code answered a question it had no business answering.

## What's in it

**The decision path lost its flat half.** 971 → 232 lines. I've written the argument as a pattern rather than as your preference, because I think it generalises: *a fallback simpler than the thing it substitutes for is always available, so it gets chosen exactly when the real machinery has failed — when its answer is least trustworthy and least examined. And its availability removes the pressure to find out why.* A system with a silent simpler path doesn't get debugged; it gets used.

**Refusal as a first-class result**, anchored on the two defects that forced it — the temperature clamp that disguised a reversed preference law, and the numeric infinity that produced an all-NaN posterior with a tie-broken decision. Both were defensible in isolation and indefensible in context. I included the honest cost: a machine that refuses more often *looks*, from outside, like one that works less.

**The two A-kernel objections were false, not open** — and neither needed anything built to discover. The normalisation theorem was already sitting in a file we had, stated for arbitrary rates; nobody had noticed. The tractability objection dissolved against the factorisation. I wrote that up as not reflecting well on us, because it doesn't: two load-bearing blockers were unexamined assumptions that didn't survive the first serious look. It's the most transferable finding of the period.

**F is deliberately not wired, and that's a result rather than a gap.** With the sharpest form included: the do-nothing candidate's number is *correct* — its predicted future is the present — and every acting candidate's is wrong. The apparent preference for inaction was one right answer beating a field of wrong ones.

**What slowed us down**, which answers your question from two turns ago in a form readers can use. Five separate readers of the registry had each encoded an assumption it later outgrew. The pattern-relevant part is the contrast between gates that **refuse** what they don't understand and gates that **report** it as a data discrepancy: the refusing ones cost an hour each; the reporting one cost a day, because a reported discrepancy invites you to go and fix data that wasn't wrong.
